posts.author: Martin123
posts.content_md:
Hello everyone!

I have to write an essay for school about computer generated holograms. I searched the web for reconstructed pictures of cgh and c++ algorithm (i have to write an application to create the holograms too) but i never found an image of a hologram with depth. I found some examples of words like "Laser" or something like this, but all of the pictures were 2D and not 3D. Since there was no example of an 3d object and its hologram, I have a few questions:

1. Can you computer generate holograms of 3d objects with an easy application as MedCosm CGHMaker (it supports z-coordinates when you pick an *.xml file)

2. What will the reconstruction look like? Will you be able to recognize the object as a real hologram?

Thank you very much for your answers. I searched the web and also your forum, but found nothing for this problem.

Martin

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
The problem will be in how will you print the image. You can generate an image with depth but then you will need to print it to a transparency. The limit of your printers abilities will be the limiting factor. If you look at the equations for off axis transmision holography you will find that 600lpi is not very good. Look for Ed Wesly's great article in the wiki for some of the simple math.

In order to make the program you require you will need to be very familiar with an FFT.

posts.author: Martin123
posts.content_md: Thank you for your answer it helped a lot.

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Martin123,

Yes, there are many examples of computer-generated holograms with impressive depth. A recent example is that quite a few were made at the MIT Media Laboratory's Spatial Imaging Group. Many of their publications were made available on their website.

Otherwise, this is an area in which you'll need access to a good library (or a school with access to online journal databases) for the "real articles." Do you have access to such things? If so I'd be happy to point you at a few. However, they all require a fairly good knowledge of math and optics.

Gregg
